title: Indian-Origin Couple Gives $20 Million to Build AI College at UNT
excerpt: Anuradha and Vikas Sinha's gift — the couple's third major donation to the university — will establish the Anuradha and Vikas Sinha College of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Analytics at the University of North Texas.
body:
• Anuradha and Vikas Sinha have donated $20 million to the University of North Texas to advance AI and advanced analytics.
  • UNT will name its new college the Anuradha and Vikas Sinha College of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Analytics.
  • The gift creates six permanent endowments covering college leadership, student scholarships, endowed professorships, entrepreneurship and incubation, advanced research and emerging technologies.
  • The college will house two academic divisions and the Applied Artificial Intelligence and Data Science Institute, uniting AI, cybersecurity, data science and health informatics under one roof.

A Landmark Gift in Denton

DENTON, Texas — A $20 million gift from Anuradha and Vikas Sinha will accelerate the University of North Texas' work in artificial intelligence and advanced analytics, creating new opportunities for students and faculty in fields rapidly reshaping industries, professions and society. In recognition of the couple's commitment, UNT will name its new college the Anuradha and Vikas Sinha College of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Analytics — an academic hub focused on the development, application and responsible use of AI, intelligent systems and data analytics.

"Artificial intelligence will be one of the defining technologies of our generation, and universities have an essential role to play in preparing the people who will shape its future. What excites us about UNT's vision is that this college will go beyond teaching students how to use AI. It will prepare them to build it, understand it, question it, govern it and apply it responsibly — developing both the builders and the stewards of intelligent systems."

— Vikas Sinha ('23 Ph.D.)

Context and Background: From Civil Engineering to Broadcom

For the Sinhas, the gift is personal. Both earned bachelor's degrees in civil engineering from Sri Venkateswara University in India before coming to the United States to continue their education. They earned graduate degrees from Florida Atlantic University, and Vikas went on to Northwestern University before earning his Ph.D. in information science with a concentration in data science from UNT in 2023. He now serves as vice president of the Mainframe Software Division at Broadcom and has served on UNT's College of Information Leadership Board since 2023.

The $20 million commitment is the couple's third major gift to UNT. In 2024, they funded the Anuradha and Vikas Sinha Department of Data Science, along with endowments supporting scholarships, faculty, research and special initiatives. A year later, they made another major gift creating the Sinha Innovation Lab for Data Science.

Impact and Analysis: Six Endowments, Two Divisions, One Institute

The gift will create six permanent endowments supporting college leadership, student scholarships, endowed professorships, entrepreneurship and incubation, advanced research and emerging technologies — advancing UNT's priorities around student success, research and innovation while preparing graduates for a workforce increasingly shaped by AI and data.

Structurally, the college will unite programs spanning artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, data science, advanced data analytics, health informatics, information science, library science and learning technologies. It will be organized into two academic divisions — Applied Intelligence and Informatics, focused on building and deploying intelligent systems, and Information and Learning Applications, focused on how those systems operate within human and institutional contexts — and will house the Applied Artificial Intelligence and Data Science Institute to connect AI research across the university and foster industry partnerships.

The timing matters. UNT's Board of Regents approved a bachelor's degree in artificial intelligence earlier this year, making UNT one of the first universities in Texas to offer such a program. The gift also strengthens UNT's capacity to compete for research funding at a moment of significant investment in Texas public research universities through the Texas University Fund.

Diaspora Angle

The Sinhas framed their gift around the immigrant experience. "For us, this gift is about paying that opportunity forward and recognizing that immigrants don't simply participate in the American dream — they help build it," Vikas said.

"International students come to our universities to learn, but their impact extends far beyond the degrees they earn. They contribute ideas, build companies, create jobs, lead communities, and create opportunities for the generations who follow them."

— Harrison Keller, Ph.D., UNT President

The gift lands as international student enrollment at UNT has declined sharply — graduate international students fell from about 6,200 in fall 2024 to about 3,400 in fall 2025, a drop that contributed to a budget shortfall and cost-cutting, according to reporting on the university.

What's Next

UNT plans to hold a campus celebration honoring the naming of the new college later this year, bringing together the Sinha family, students, faculty, university leaders and community members. With the college structure taking shape and endowments funding leadership, scholarships and research, the next test will be recruiting — outstanding faculty, industry partners, and the students who will become, as the college intends, both builders and stewards of intelligent systems.
